title: Uncle Tom’s Cabin
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
setting: A Kentucky farm, the Ohio river and the free states, New Orleans, and a cotton plantation on the Red River
lengthNote: Forty-five chapters in two volumes, written to a weekly newspaper deadline
openingLine: Late in the afternoon of a chilly day in February, two gentlemen were sitting alone over their wine, in a well-furnished dining parlor, in the town of P⁠⸺, in Kentucky.
summary: A Kentucky farmer in debt sells two people to settle it, and the novel follows both of them in opposite directions. Eliza runs north with her child across the ice of the Ohio; Tom is carried south through three owners until he reaches a plantation where the arithmetic of cotton makes a man cheaper to replace than to keep. Stowe built the book out of scenes designed to be unbearable to a churchgoing readership, and then told that readership what it was to do about them.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Uncle Tom’s Cabin
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously in Roman numerals from I to XLV across the two volumes of the 1852 book edition; references below give the chapter only.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Weekly in the abolitionist paper The National Era, where it ran far longer than the few instalments originally intended.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Two volumes from John P. Jewett of Boston, published while the serial was still finishing.

atAGlance.label: The law behind it
atAGlance.note: It obliged citizens of free states to assist in returning people who had escaped, which is why so much of the novel is set in northern parlours.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Eliza moves north and out of the book's jurisdiction; Tom moves south and deeper into it. Neither plot resolves the other.

structure.label: Chapters I–VIII
structure.title: A debt, and two people sold to cover it
structure.summary: Mr Shelby, who considers himself a kind man, settles his accounts by selling Tom and the child Harry to a trader. Eliza overhears the arrangement and runs that night; Tom, who could run, stays because leaving would mean the rest of the estate going instead. The novel's whole argument is set up in a dining parlour before anybody is cruel to anyone.

scenes.title: The bargain
scenes.summary: Haley and Shelby over the wine; Eliza listens at the door; George Harris tells his wife he will not endure it much longer.

scenes.title: The cabin and the flight
scenes.summary: An evening of hymn-singing in Tom's cabin, then Eliza waking Harry at midnight and the household covering for her.

scenes.title: The ice
scenes.summary: Eliza crosses the Ohio on the breaking floes, and the slave-catchers are hired in a tavern.

structure.label: Chapters IX–XIII
structure.title: Free states, and a boat going the other way
structure.summary: The chapters alternate between the fugitives and their cargo counterpart. A senator who voted for the Fugitive Slave Act finds it in his kitchen; George Harris faces down his pursuers on a rock; and Haley, on a steamboat south, sells a woman's infant off her lap and records the consequence in his account book.

scenes.title: Senator Bird
scenes.summary: Mrs Bird argues the law down in her own parlour, and the senator drives Eliza to a safe house himself.

scenes.title: Two directions at once
scenes.summary: Tom is taken from his family and shipped downriver; George Harris, in disguise, declares himself a man without a country.

scenes.title: The Quaker settlement
scenes.summary: Rachel Halliday's kitchen: the novel's model household, run without owning anybody.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVIII
structure.title: New Orleans, and a household that means well
structure.summary: Tom saves a child who falls overboard and is bought by her father, and the book's middle section installs him in the most comfortable slavery it can imagine. Augustine St Clare talks brilliantly against the system he profits from; his cousin Ophelia arrives from Vermont opposed to slavery and unable to bear the people held under it.

scenes.title: Eva and the boat
scenes.summary: Tom is bought after pulling Evangeline St Clare out of the Mississippi.

scenes.title: The St Clare house
scenes.summary: Marie's invalidism, Ophelia's efficiency, and St Clare's long argument that knowing better changes nothing.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXVIII
structure.title: Two deaths, and the paper that was never signed
structure.summary: St Clare sets out the economics of ownership more clearly than any abolitionist in the book and does nothing. Ophelia is given Topsy to educate and discovers her own revulsion. Eva dies at length and in public, as sentimental fiction required; her father is stabbed in a tavern brawl before he can free Tom, and the household is sold.

scenes.title: The argument
scenes.summary: St Clare on his brother's plantation, on his own idleness, and on what the law actually permits.

scenes.title: Ophelia and Topsy
scenes.summary: A northern woman's antislavery principle meets a child she cannot bring herself to touch.

scenes.title: Two funerals
scenes.summary: Eva's death, St Clare's sudden one, and Marie's decision to sell.

structure.label: Chapters XXIX–XXXVIII
structure.title: The Red River, where manners stop
structure.summary: Tom is sold at auction to Simon Legree and taken to a plantation run on the principle that people are cheaper to work to death than to maintain. Cassy, who has survived it longest, tells Tom her history; Legree, who is afraid of nothing visible, turns out to be terrified of a lock of hair and a noise in the garret.

scenes.title: The warehouse and the wagon
scenes.summary: The New Orleans sale rooms, and the journey upriver with Legree's new purchases.

scenes.title: Legree's arithmetic
scenes.summary: Tom refuses to flog a sick woman; Cassy gives the plantation's history in her own voice.

scenes.title: The garret
scenes.summary: Legree's superstition, Cassy's plan, and Tom's refusal to say where the women have gone.

structure.label: Chapters XXXIX–XLV
structure.title: An escape, a death and an address to the reader
structure.summary: Cassy and Emmeline hide in the haunted garret while the plantation searches the swamp for them. Tom is beaten to death for his silence, and George Shelby arrives two days late with the money to buy him. The scattered family is reassembled improbably, sails for Liberia, and Stowe steps forward to tell her readers what she wants them to do.

scenes.title: The ghost in the garret
scenes.summary: Cassy uses Legree's superstition against him; Tom is flogged and dies; George Shelby buries him.

scenes.title: Reunions
scenes.summary: Cassy discovers that Eliza is her daughter; the Harrises decide on Liberia; George Shelby frees the people at home.

scenes.title: Concluding remarks
scenes.summary: Stowe drops the fiction, states which incidents are drawn from record, and addresses the mothers of America directly.

characters.name: Tom
characters.role: An enslaved man, sold three times in the course of the novel
characters.summary: He is a literate, married man of about forty who reads his Bible slowly with a finger, and the novel's central question is whether his refusal to escape is obedience or a decision. On the Red River he draws a line and will not move it, and the line costs him his life rather than saving it.
characters.clue: He could have run north with the others and did not, because the rest of the estate would have been sold instead; he is killed for refusing to say where two women went.

characters.name: Eliza Harris
characters.role: An enslaved woman in the Shelby household, Harry's mother
characters.summary: She is given the novel's most famous physical action and almost none of its dialogue about principle: she hears the sale discussed through a door and is over the river before anyone has finished arguing. Everything she does afterwards is organised around keeping a five-year-old alive and quiet.
characters.clue: She crossed a river full of moving ice with a child on her hip, and a slave-catcher watching from the bank called the jump the best he had ever seen.

characters.name: George Harris
characters.role: Eliza's husband, hired out to a factory by his owner
characters.summary: He invented a machine for cleaning hemp and was taken out of the factory for it, which is the novel's compressed statement of what slavery wastes. He argues rather than endures, arms himself, and is the one character allowed to reject the country outright rather than appeal to its conscience.
characters.clue: A factory hand whose invention got him sent back to field work, he stands on a rock above a pursuing posse and declares that he has no country at all.

characters.name: Haley
characters.summary: Stowe makes him neither a monster nor an aberration but a man with a business model, who prides himself on humane methods because damaged goods sell badly. He supplies the novel's running joke and its coldest passages: the same voice that talks about conscience keeps a ledger of losses.
characters.clue: He boasts of his humanity in the trade, and enters a woman who has drowned herself in his account book under the heading of losses.

characters.name: Mrs Shelby
characters.summary: She has taught the people she owns to read and to pray and believes this makes the arrangement tolerable; the sale shows her that her opinions have no legal force whatever. Her outrage is genuine and completely ineffective, which is the use Stowe makes of her.
characters.clue: She taught them their catechism and their letters, and found on the morning of the sale that her husband had not consulted her and did not need to.

characters.name: Augustine St Clare
characters.role: A New Orleans gentleman, Tom's second owner
characters.summary: He can describe the economics and the hypocrisy of slavery better than anyone else in the novel, and he keeps a household of people he has not freed. Stowe gives the clearest analysis to a man who will not act on it, which makes his sudden death the most pointed thing that happens in the book.
characters.clue: He calls the whole business accursed of God and man over his brandy, and dies with the manumission papers still unsigned.

characters.name: Evangeline St Clare
characters.summary: She is the novel's sentimental engine: a child who says the unanswerable thing and then dies of it slowly enough for everyone to gather. Readers who find her unbearable and readers who weep over her are responding to the same technique, which Stowe deploys with complete deliberation.
characters.clue: A child who tells a grown man she would die for the people he owns, and then does — over most of a chapter, with the household assembled.

characters.name: Miss Ophelia
characters.summary: She arrives with northern antislavery opinions and a horror of disorder, and the novel uses her to make the point it most wanted its readers to feel: that opposing slavery in principle and being unable to touch a black child are perfectly compatible. Her slow correction by Topsy is the only conversion in the book that takes work.
characters.clue: A New Englander who disapproved of slavery all her life, and had to be taught by a child that she could not bear to be in the same room as the people she pitied.

relationships.label: given charge of, and educated by

characters.name: Topsy
characters.role: A child in the St Clare household
characters.summary: She answers questions about her origins by saying she had none, and the answer is the most efficient indictment of the trade in the novel. She is also the character in whom Stowe's comic writing comes closest to the minstrel stage, and the two facts have to be held together rather than traded off.
characters.clue: Asked who made her, she says she has no father, no mother and no birth, and supposes she was raised by a speculator.

characters.name: Simon Legree
characters.role: A cotton planter on the Red River, Tom's last owner
characters.summary: He runs his plantation on a stated policy of using people up and buying more, and he sets the enslaved to guard each other so that nobody can be trusted. Stowe makes him a New Englander by birth, which quietly removes the comfort of treating him as a southern problem.
characters.clue: He works people to death on principle because replacements are cheaper than upkeep, and is frightened out of his wits by a lock of hair and a noise upstairs.

characters.name: Cassy
characters.role: An enslaved woman on Legree's plantation
characters.summary: She has been educated, sold repeatedly, separated from three children and driven to kill an infant rather than let it be sold, and she tells all of it herself in the first person. She is also the only person in the novel who defeats a white man by out-thinking him, using his own fear of the house against him.
characters.clue: She reads her owner's terrors better than he does, and escapes by hiding in the one room on the plantation he will not enter.

themes.name: Law, debt and property in people
themes.summary: Stowe's method is to show ownership working through ordinary paperwork rather than through the whip: a debt, a bill of sale, an unsigned deed of manumission, a statute obliging a senator's neighbours to help recapture a stranger. The cruelty of the Red River is the same legal power that the Shelbys exercise politely.
themes.development: A private debt in Chapter I, the Fugitive Slave Act in Senator Bird's parlour, St Clare's failure to sign in Chapter XXVIII, and the auction rooms of Chapter XXX where the law and the market are the same thing.

themes.name: Feeling as political argument
themes.summary: The book asks its readers to imagine an enslaved family through the domestic affections they already honour, and then to act on the recognition. Every device of popular fiction — the deathbed, the lost child, the reunion — is turned toward a legislative end, and the concluding chapter says so explicitly.
themes.development: From the sale overheard in Chapter I, through Eva's death, to the direct instruction in Chapter XLV that the least a reader can do is to see to it that they feel rightly.

themes.name: Christianity on trial
themes.summary: Nearly every character has a religion and the novel spends its length distinguishing between them: the piety that sanctions a sale, the piety that sings hymns in a cabin, the northern church that deplores slavery and returns fugitives. Stowe's final pages put the account squarely at the door of the American churches.
themes.development: Tom's Bible in Chapter IV, Mrs Bird against her husband's vote in Chapter IX, St Clare's mockery of clerical apologists, Legree's use of scripture as a licence, and the judgement pronounced in Chapter XLV.

themes.name: Mothers and children
themes.summary: The novel's engine is separation: a child sold off a lap on a steamboat, a mother crossing broken ice, a woman who poisoned her own infant rather than see it sold, and a reader addressed at the end as a mother who has stood beside a cradle. Stowe treats the destruction of families as slavery's defining product rather than its excess.
themes.development: Eliza's flight in Chapter VII, the unnamed woman on Haley's boat in Chapter XII, Cassy's history in Chapter XXXIV, and the address to the mothers of America in Chapter XLV.

themes.name: Flight and the geography of freedom
themes.summary: North and south are not moral categories in this book but distances with laws attached. Eliza's route runs through Ohio parlours where the Fugitive Slave Act reaches, and ends outside the country altogether; Tom's runs downriver through kinder and kinder owners into the worst place in the novel.
themes.development: The river crossing in Chapter VII, the Quaker settlement in Chapter XIII, George's declaration on the rock in Chapter XVII, and the decision in Chapter XLIII to leave for Liberia rather than stay in a country that will not have them.

themes.name: Race, type and caricature
themes.summary: Stowe assigns temperaments by descent — Tom's patience, George's intellect explained by a white father, Topsy's comic energy — and the novel's sympathy runs along those lines rather than across them. This is the book's deepest and most enduring problem, and it is present in the same scenes that made it politically effective.
themes.development: The narrator's generalisations about African nature in the New Orleans chapters, the handling of Topsy, the whiteness of the characters permitted to argue and escape, and the Liberian ending that removes the freed family from America altogether.

techniques.name: The double plot
techniques.definition: Two parallel stories arranged so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Eliza going north and Tom going south are told in alternating blocks, so that every act of the flight plot is read against a corresponding stage of the sale plot, and neither is allowed to stand for the whole.

techniques.name: Address to the reader
techniques.definition: Turning from the narrative to speak to the person holding the book.
techniques.inThisBook: Stowe interrupts constantly — to tell a trader's reader that his own heart could be brought to the same place, and finally to address the mothers of America by name in the closing chapter.

techniques.name: The tableau
techniques.definition: A scene composed and held still so that its emotional meaning can be read off it.
techniques.inThisBook: The deathbeds, the cabin at hymn-time, the auction block, the child handed across a wagon seat: scenes arranged with the stillness of an engraving, which is one reason the book moved so easily onto the stage.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.inThisBook: Stowe writes four or five distinct speech registers — Kentucky field, New Orleans drawing room, Vermont, Quaker plain speech — and uses the gap between them to mark exactly how much education each character has been allowed.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Using scripture as the ground of an argument rather than as decoration.
techniques.inThisBook: Characters quote the same verses at each other for opposite purposes — Legree citing servants obeying masters, Tom answering out of the Gospels — so that the novel stages a dispute about interpretation rather than about belief.

techniques.name: Weekly serial structure
techniques.definition: A narrative shaped by instalments, each needing its own crisis.
techniques.inThisBook: Written to a weekly deadline for The National Era, the book keeps two plots alive by cutting between them, and its most famous set pieces sit exactly where an instalment had to end.

quotations.text: Well, I’ve got just as much conscience as any man in business can afford to keep
quotations.speaker: Haley
quotations.context: The trader, over wine, negotiating the sale of Tom and the child Harry.
quotations.analysis: Conscience is presented as an overhead, priced like any other, and the joke is that the speaker is entirely sincere. Stowe puts the novel's economic case in its first pages and in the mouth of its least reflective character, so that everything said later by thoughtful men is an elaboration of a trader's small talk.

quotations.text: a delicately formed hand and a trim foot and ankle were items of appearance that did not escape the quick eye of the trader, well used to run up at a glance the points of a fine female article.
quotations.context: Eliza has come into the parlour on an errand and gone out again.
quotations.analysis: The sentence begins as a conventional novelistic description of a pretty woman and ends in the vocabulary of livestock, with 'items' and 'points' and 'article' doing the turn. The reader is made to notice that they have been looking at her in the same way the trader has, one clause earlier.

quotations.text: I always thought that I must obey my master and mistress, or I couldn’t be a Christian.
quotations.speaker: Eliza
quotations.context: To George, who has told her he intends to escape.
quotations.analysis: She states the doctrine she has been taught as a condition of her faith, and within four chapters she will break it with a child on her hip. The novel gets its Christian readers to abandon that teaching by letting a good woman hold it first, and then making obedience unthinkable.

quotations.text: It is a sin to hold a slave under laws like ours
quotations.speaker: Mrs Shelby
quotations.context: On learning that her husband has sold Tom and Harry to settle a debt.
quotations.analysis: The qualification is the whole sentence: it is the laws that make it a sin, which leaves open the idea of a slavery conducted decently. Stowe gives her heroine the argument most of her readers actually held, and then spends forty chapters dismantling it by following the paperwork.

quotations.text: God helping me, I crossed on the ice
quotations.speaker: Eliza
quotations.context: In Senator Bird's kitchen, answering the disbelief of everyone in the room.
quotations.analysis: The novel's most spectacular action is reported afterwards, flatly, by the person who performed it, and the room's astonishment does the work that description would. Note that she credits God and the syntax credits herself: the main verb is hers, and the help is a subordinate phrase.

quotations.text: It’s a shameful, wicked, abominable law, and I’ll break it, for one, the first time I get a chance
quotations.speaker: Mrs Bird
quotations.context: To her husband, who has voted for the Fugitive Slave Act.
quotations.analysis: Three adjectives and then a plan, which is the order Stowe wants her readers to follow. The chapter is constructed so that the opportunity arrives within the hour, and the senator who defended the law in the abstract is soon driving a wagon through the mud at midnight.

quotations.text: Mr. Wilson, you have a country; but what country have I, or anyone like me, born of slave mothers?
quotations.speaker: George Harris
quotations.context: In an inn, in disguise, to his former employer from the factory.
quotations.analysis: The question is put to a sympathetic man who has just advised obedience to the law, and it works by simple grammatical contrast: you have, what have I. Stowe lets George reject the national argument rather than appeal to it, which is why he ends the novel outside the United States.

quotations.text: I’ll fight for my liberty to the last breath I breathe. You say your fathers did it; if it was right for them, it is right for me!
quotations.speaker: George Harris
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, having announced that he is armed.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask for the revolution's principles to be extended to him; he points out that they already cover his case and dares his listener to deny it. An American readership in 1852 could refuse the claim only by unsaying its own founding story, which is precisely the trap the sentence sets.

quotations.text: The trader, therefore, sat discontentedly down, with his little account-book, and put down the missing body and soul under the head of losses!
quotations.context: After a woman whose child Haley has sold has gone over the side of the steamboat.
quotations.analysis: A suicide is recorded as a bookkeeping entry, and the sentence adopts the ledger's own calm until the last three words. 'Body and soul' is the trade's own phrase used against it: the column exists because the law allows a soul to be entered as stock.

quotations.text: His heart was exactly where yours, sir, and mine could be brought, with proper effort and cultivation.
quotations.context: Of Haley, who has just watched a mother lose her child without interest.
quotations.analysis: The narrator turns from the trader to the reader mid-paragraph and includes herself in the indictment, which stops the sentence from being a simple accusation. 'Cultivation' is the word a Victorian reader would apply to their own moral improvement, redeployed here to describe the process of learning not to care.

quotations.text: You loathe them as you would a snake or a toad, yet you are indignant at their wrongs.
quotations.speaker: Augustine St Clare
quotations.context: To his cousin Ophelia, on the difference between northern and southern feeling.
quotations.analysis: The line is aimed past Ophelia at the book's actual readership, most of whom lived north of the Ohio and had subscribed to an antislavery paper. Stowe puts her sharpest attack on her own supporters into the mouth of a slaveholder, which makes it harder to dismiss and impossible to enjoy.

quotations.text: This cursed business, accursed of God and man, what is it?
quotations.speaker: Augustine St Clare
quotations.context: Beginning a long explanation of slavery to Ophelia, in his own house, with his own servants in it.
quotations.analysis: He asks the question rhetorically and then answers it in the language of force rather than of race: because I am strong and he is weak, therefore I may. The speech is the most complete argument in the novel, and it is given to the one man in a position to act who never does.

quotations.text: never had no father nor mother, nor nothin’. I was raised by a speculator, with lots of others.
quotations.speaker: Topsy
quotations.context: Answering Ophelia's questions about where she comes from.
quotations.analysis: The scene is played for comedy and the answer is a statement of fact about the domestic trade, which is exactly the difficulty Topsy presents. 'Raised by a speculator' names the only parent the market provided, and the sentence is funny and unanswerable in the same breath.

quotations.text: I would die for them, Tom, if I could
quotations.speaker: Eva St Clare
quotations.context: To Tom in the garden, having heard the stories of the people in the household.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is doing something odd: she is already dying, and the novel is about to spend a chapter arranging her death as a redemptive event. Stowe's sentimental machinery is at its most exposed here — a child's willingness to die is offered as the emotional equivalent of the political act nobody in the house will perform.

quotations.text: Mas’r, if you mean to kill me, kill me; but, as to my raising my hand agin anyone here, I never shall
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: Refusing Legree's order to flog a sick woman in the field.
quotations.analysis: The refusal is not to be beaten but to beat, and that distinction is the whole of Tom's position: he concedes the body and withholds the act. Legree's plantation runs on making the enslaved police each other, so one man declining to strike is a structural problem rather than a moral gesture.

quotations.text: No! no! no! my soul an’t yours, Mas’r! You haven’t bought it
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: Answering Legree's demand to know whether he is not his master's, body and soul.
quotations.analysis: Legree has just cited scripture and a purchase price; Tom answers the property claim in property language, conceding the sale and disputing what was in it. The triple 'no' is the only moment in the novel where Tom raises his voice, and he does it about a point of law.

quotations.text: I’ve been on this place five years, body and soul, under this man’s foot; and I hate him as I do the devil!
quotations.speaker: Cassy
quotations.context: Telling Tom what the plantation is, on the night after his first flogging.
quotations.analysis: She uses the same phrase Tom has just refused to concede, and she concedes it, which measures the distance between them. Stowe gives Cassy the plainest hatred in the book and does not require her to repent of it, even while the novel is arranging Tom's forgiveness.

quotations.text: in the judgment day, I will stand up before God, a witness against those that have ruined me and my children, body and soul!
quotations.speaker: Cassy
quotations.context: The end of her account of her own life, told to Tom in the first person.
quotations.analysis: She does not ask the reader for pity; she declares herself a witness in a proceeding that has not yet opened. It is the strongest claim to legal personality in the novel, and it is made by a woman whose testimony no court in Louisiana would have heard.

quotations.text: I’ll give ye all the work of my hands, all my time, all my strength; but my soul I won’t give up to mortal man.
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: To Legree, who has told him he is broken and offers him a place as an overseer.
quotations.analysis: The offer on the table is promotion — Legree wants Tom to drive the others — so the refusal is of power rather than of suffering. The list of what he concedes is long and specific, which makes the single withheld item look like a legal reservation rather than a pious formula.

quotations.text: they can see to it that they feel right
quotations.context: In the concluding remarks, answering the question of what any individual can do.
quotations.analysis: It is the most-quoted sentence in the book and the most criticised, because it makes the reader's inner state the unit of political action. Read in context it is less passive than it sounds — the paragraph goes on to talk about influence and atmosphere — but the novel does end by asking for feeling and leaving the legislation to follow.

quotations.text: And say, mothers of America, is this a thing to be defended, sympathized with, passed over in silence?
quotations.context: The closing appeal, after a page addressed to farmers, sailors and shipowners by region.
quotations.analysis: Stowe names her actual constituency last and most directly, and the three verbs run from active approval to mere silence, closing every available position. The fiction has been put down by this point: the last chapter is a pamphlet, and the novel has been its evidence.

quotations.text: not surer is the eternal law by which the millstone sinks in the ocean, than that stronger law, by which injustice and cruelty shall bring on nations the wrath of Almighty God!
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a physical certainty, so judgement is presented as mechanics rather than as a threat. Nine years before the first shots, Stowe ends a domestic novel by telling the United States that the consequence is already in motion and that repentance is the only variable left.

timeline.label: Harriet Beecher born in Litchfield, Connecticut
timeline.detail: Into a famous clerical family; her father Lyman Beecher and several brothers were preachers.

timeline.label: The Beechers move to Cincinnati
timeline.detail: Eighteen years living on the Ohio, across the river from a slave state, supplied most of what she knew at first hand.

timeline.label: Marriage to Calvin Stowe
timeline.detail: A biblical scholar; the couple later moved to Brunswick, Maine, where the novel was begun.

timeline.label: The Fugitive Slave Act
timeline.detail: Part of the Compromise of 1850, it required citizens of free states to assist in recapture and is the immediate provocation for the book.

timeline.label: Serialisation begins in The National Era
timeline.detail: From June, in an abolitionist weekly in Washington; the story ran far beyond its planned length.

timeline.label: Published in two volumes by John P. Jewett
timeline.detail: It sold on a scale no American novel had reached before, and was pirated and translated across Europe within the year.

timeline.label: The first stage versions appear
timeline.detail: Unlicensed dramatisations began at once; the 'Tom shows' outlived the book's reputation and coarsened everything in it.

timeline.label: A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin
timeline.detail: Stowe answered accusations of invention by publishing the court records, advertisements and narratives behind her scenes.

timeline.label: The Dred Scott decision
timeline.detail: The Supreme Court held that a black American could not be a citizen, hardening the argument the novel had entered.

timeline.label: The American Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The story that Lincoln greeted Stowe as the little woman who started the war is undocumented and long-lived.

timeline.label: The Thirteenth Amendment
timeline.detail: Slavery abolished in the United States, thirteen years after the book appeared.

timeline.label: Stowe dies at Hartford, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then the novel's stage afterlife had largely replaced the book in the public mind.

places.name: Maysville, Kentucky
places.note: The Ohio-river country north of Lexington that Stowe knew, and the setting of the Shelby farm at the novel's opening.

places.name: Ripley, Ohio
places.note: The free-state bank of the Ohio opposite Kentucky; a crossing of this kind is the model for Eliza's.

places.name: Cincinnati
places.note: Where Stowe lived for eighteen years, and the city through which the northern chapters' traffic in people and rumour passes.

places.name: New Orleans
places.note: The St Clare household, and the auction rooms where Tom is sold after St Clare's death.

places.name: Alexandria, Louisiana
places.note: On the Red River, the region in which Legree's isolated cotton plantation is placed.

places.name: Brunswick, Maine
places.note: Where Stowe was living when she began writing, after the Fugitive Slave Act reached into the free states.

criticalViews.summary: On any measure of effect this is the most consequential American novel of the nineteenth century: it put the domestic slave trade in front of a mass readership that had been able to think of slavery as a distant arrangement, and it made the Fugitive Slave Act a matter of personal conduct rather than policy.
criticalViews.counter: Effect is not the same as accuracy or fairness, and the book's power came partly from techniques — the dying child, the loyal servant — that later did real damage.

criticalViews.position: The objection to its racial typing
criticalViews.summary: The long-standing critical objection is that Stowe's sympathy runs along a racial map: patience and piety are given to Tom as qualities of descent, intellect and rebellion belong to the characters with white fathers, and Topsy is written for laughter in a register the minstrel stage had already established.
criticalViews.counter: The typology was the common property of the period and Stowe used it to move readers who shared it, which is an explanation of the method rather than a defence of it.

criticalViews.summary: Critics since the 1980s have taken the sentimental machinery seriously as a strategy rather than a failing, arguing that domestic feeling was one of the few forms of public authority available to women writers, and that the book was engineered to convert emotion into votes and subscriptions.
criticalViews.counter: The method's limit is stated in the book itself: the final advice to the individual reader is to feel rightly, which asks less than the situation the novel has just described.

criticalViews.summary: For a century the stage versions — unlicensed, altered, often openly racist — were far more widely seen than the novel, and the insult that the name later carried was manufactured largely by them rather than by Stowe's pages.
criticalViews.counter: Separating the two only goes so far: the character's endurance and death are in the novel, and a modern reader still has to decide what the book is asking of him.

criticalViews.summary: Read next to Douglass's Narrative, published seven years earlier, the novel's status changes: Stowe invents and arranges in order to persuade, while Douglass gives names and counties and can be checked.
criticalViews.counter: Stowe answered the charge of invention in 1853 with A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin, setting out the advertisements, trials and narratives behind her scenes.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel make slavery a matter of law and money rather than of individual cruelty?
essayQuestions.focus: Debt, contract and the Fugitive Slave Act
plan: Begin with Chapter I: a decent man, a creditor and an ordinary contract are enough to destroy two families.
Follow Haley's account book through Chapter XII, where a death is entered under losses.
Use Senator Bird's kitchen to show the 1850 Act reaching into a free state and a private house.
Weigh St Clare, who understands everything and signs nothing, against Legree, who signs everything and understands nothing.
Close by asking what the ending implies about remedy: individual manumission, or a change in the law.

essayQuestions.question: 'Its abolitionist force and its racial typing are in the same sentences.' Discuss.
plan: Set out the case for the book's effect: the scale of its readership and the specific political provocation it answered.
Examine how sympathy is distributed — who argues, who escapes, who endures, and how that maps onto descent in the narrator's own commentary.
Read the Topsy scenes closely, holding the comic register and the documentary content together.
Consider St Clare's attack on northern squeamishness as evidence that Stowe understood at least part of the problem.
Reach a judgement that does not require choosing between historical importance and the objection.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of telling Eliza's story and Tom's story at the same time?
plan: Map the alternation: which chapters belong to the flight and which to the descent.
Show how each plot supplies what the other lacks — speed and hope against endurance and analysis.
Note that the two plots never meet again, and that only one of them ends in freedom.
Consider the serial deadline as a formal cause of the cutting between them.
Ask what the novel would argue if either half were removed.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel use Christianity, and against whom?
essayQuestions.focus: Scripture, the churches and the last chapter
plan: Distinguish the several religions in the book: Tom's, Mrs Bird's, Legree's use of scripture, and the northern churches at a distance.
Analyse the exchange in Chapter XXXIII, where a purchase price and a Bible verse are produced together.
Set Cassy's refusal to forgive beside Tom's forgiveness, and ask whether the novel treats them as equals.
Use the concluding remarks to show where Stowe finally lays the charge.
Compare Douglass's appendix of 1845, which makes the same distinction from the inside.

discussionQuestions: Tom could have escaped with Eliza and does not. Is that obedience, calculation, or something the novel cannot quite name?
St Clare understands slavery better than any abolitionist in the book and frees nobody. Why does Stowe give the best argument to that character?
The novel's most famous advice is that readers should see to it that they feel rightly. Is that enough, and did Stowe think it was?
Topsy's answers about her origins are played for laughter and are factually exact. How should a reader now hold those two things together?
The freed family sails for Liberia at the end. What does that ending concede about the country the book is addressing?

related.why: The first-person testimony published seven years earlier, and the book against which Stowe's inventions have always been measured.
The same river and the same law thirty years later, with a boy deciding to break it and calling the decision wickedness.
Twain on descent, the one-drop rule and the legal fictions of race, written after emancipation had settled nothing.
Published two years earlier: another American novel about public judgement, the churches, and a woman's standing before them.
The other great weekly serial of the period, and a useful comparison for how instalment deadlines shape a plot.
